newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin leaves hospital after pneumonia treatment.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin leaves hospital after pneumonia treatment.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin left hospital on Monday after 12 days of treatment for pneumonia, but a spokesman said he would not be rushing back to the Kremlin.

"The in-patient stage of Boris Nikolayevich's treatment for double pneumonia is finishing today and the president is transferring to the Gorky-9 residence near Moscow where his treatment will continue," presidential press secretary Sergei Yaztrzhembsky told a news briefing.

A Kremlin spokesman later confirmed that Yeltsin had left the hospital at about six o'clock (1500 GMT) after reporters saw a fleet of black official cars sweep down the elite hospital's snowy driveway.

The chief doctor treating Yeltsin said last week that the 65-year-old Kremlin leader, under pressure from his political rivals to step down over his ill health, was anxious to leave hospital as soon as possible.
His move will ease that pressure but despite the steady recovery reported by the Kremlin, Russian observers are beginning to wonder how long he will be able to cling to power.

"There is no point in expecting the president to rush back to full-time work, which also means the Kremlin," Yasztrzhembsky said, despite the doubts over Yeltsin's ability to rule after six months out of the Kremlin last year with heart problems.
An influential presenter on NTV commercial television said on Sunday Russia was beginning to look to the post-Yeltsin era.

"Russians have already become aware of the sad truth that Yeltsin may never be able to work fully again, that for the remaining three years of his presidency we will be forced to live in expectation of new elections," said Yevgeny Kiselyov, who presents the the weekly current affairs programme Itogi.
While Yeltsin continued his convalescence, his foreign minister conducted the first of a new round of high-level talks on Russia's thorny relationship with NATO.
Yevgeny Primakov held a five-hour meeting with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, who came to Moscow to try to ease Russian fears over the Western alliance's expansion plans.

NATO is expected to issue invitations to the first of a list of former East Bloc countries in July and wants to soothe Russia's anger over the plan by forging a special relationship with the former superpower.

Yastrzhembsky said one should not expect much from what was just the first round of talks, but warned the West that Moscow was no longer satisfied with assurances from NATO that its expansion was not a threat.
"Russia and NATO must move to specific, hard and concrete discussions. Moscow doesn't believe in vague declarations and eloquent promises...which are not written down," he said.
"That's quite an important difference between Russia now and in 1990...The period of romanticism in diplomacy is over."
Yeltsin's last major step before going to hospital was to summon his top ministers and order them to clarify Moscow's position on NATO expansion and possible steps it might take.
A week ago he sent a letter to Russia's closest neighbour Belarus suggesting the two hold referendums on unifying, a move which some Kremlin officials said would be a good response to NATO expansion.
But Yastrzhembsky said on Monday the two were not connected.
He also dismissed the gloomy predictions about Yeltsin's future ability to work.
He read out a long list of presidential decrees which he said Yeltsin had signed and added that the Kremlin leader had spoken by telephone on Monday to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
He said the two men would probably not hold their regular meeting on Tuesday and that Yeltsin's work this week would be focused on state papers.
